transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Louise Schiavone.
A federal judge has thrown out the Trump administration's lawsuit over the U.S. Senate race in Alaska.
NPR's Hansi Lo Wang reports the administration will appeal.
The Trump administration asked the judge to block the certification results from the U.S.
Senate race in Alaska if the Republican incumbent loses.
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason found the administration does not have the ability to
bring this lawsuit.
President Trump said he ordered it to be filed because out of the four Senate candidates
on Alaska's ballot, two have similar names — the Republican incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan
and Daniel Sullivan Jr., who is not affiliated with a local party.
In June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled Daniel Sullivan Jr. has the right to run as a candidate.
A recent New York Times report that NPR has not independently confirmed says Democratic
campaign operatives were behind efforts to prop up Sullivan Jr. as a spoiler candidate.
The Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, has denied any involvement.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
In Michigan, nearly one in three voters have already cast a ballot, according to state
data, on the ballot a hotly contested U.S. Senate race with new developments today, along
with 13 U.S. House seats and statewide races.
NPR's Eric McDaniel has more.
We call it Election Day, but the reality is voting has been happening for weeks already.
Across the country, Tuesday is when voting ends.
And that's made it easier for folks to participate, but it also means that if you send in your
ballot early, you might miss a late-breaking surprise.
That's true for 29 percent of voters in Michigan who voted before U.S. Representative
Haley Stevens, a Democrat and the Senate primary opponent of Democratic pick Abdul El-Sayed,
endorsed the Republican in the race on Sunday, former Congressman Mike Rogers.
Still, millions more ballots are expected in the coming days.
Eric McDaniel, NPR News, Washington.
Today is the first day of open enrollment for the Affordable Care Act marketplaces, including
Healthcare.gov.
As NPR's Selena Simmons-Duffin reports, the markets lost millions of enrollees last year,
as the federal government stopped giving extra money for some people's premiums.
The marketplaces are designed for people who don't qualify for a public program, like Medicare
or Medicaid, and who don't get health insurance through their jobs.
Enrollment on Healthcare.gov, which is run by the federal government and all of the state-run
marketplaces, hit a record of 24 million in 2025.
This year, that number dropped by nearly 3 million.
The Trump administration claims the decline in enrollment is a result of weeding out people
who were ineligible or "fantom enrollees."
Health experts say that it's more likely due to higher costs.
Republicans in Congress declined to extend extra money that kept premiums more affordable.
Open enrollment runs until at least January 15th.
The exact deadline varies by state.
Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News in Washington.
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney is saying he had constructive talks today about a potential
trade deal with President Trump.
Trade friction between the U.S. and Canada has been a political issue for some states,
especially Michigan and Maine.
A Swedish runner secured victory in the men's competition of the New York City Marathon
today.
NPR's Chantaliz Destor reports on the annual race.
Andreas Aumgren of Sweden won the men's race one Sunday with a time of two hours, six minutes
and one second.
He beat Yaman Abraham Krippa of Italy by 13 seconds, who finished in second place.
This was both men's first New York City marathon debut.
Sheila Shevkarui, a 2024 champion from Kenya, won the women's race at two hours, 24 minutes
and 36 seconds.
Nearly 60,000 runners from around the world are estimated to have participated in the
marathon that spans 26.2 miles.
The race spanned all five boroughs and across five bridges.
Champions of the Women's and Men's Open Division will receive $100,000 each.
Champions of the Women's and Men's Wheelchair Division will receive $50,000 each.
Chantaliz Destor, NPR News.
Democratic U.S. Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut is in the hospital after having a stroke on
Saturday according to his chief of staff.
His office says his doctors are encouraged by Murphy's progress and that he is awake
and alert and expected to make a full recovery.
He'd been attending his son's hockey game when he experienced numbness in his arm.
I'm Louise Skivone, NPR News, Washington.

topics.text: Federal judge Sharon Gleason dismisses Trump administration's lawsuit over Alaska Senate race; administration to appeal
Nearly 29 percent of Michigan voters have already cast ballots in hotly contested U.S. Senate race
ACA marketplaces open enrollment today; Healthcare.gov enrollment falls nearly 3 million after federal subsidies lapse
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney says constructive trade talks held with President Trump
Sweden's Andreas Aumgren wins men's New York City Marathon; Sheila Chepkirui wins women's race
